claims.text: Cast equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and strength.
The relatively low hardness and strength of cast equimolar CoCrFeNiTi stem from a coarse, single-phase solid-solution microstructure.
The starting cast alloy has insufficient grain-boundary strengthening.
The starting cast alloy contains minimal finely dispersed secondary precipitates and therefore lacks substantial dispersion strengthening.
High-energy ball milling under argon followed by vacuum spark plasma sintering will refine the grain size of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
High-energy ball milling and spark plasma sintering will induce nanoscale secondary precipitates in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
The resulting precipitates will be fine, dispersed, and located at grain boundaries.
Grain refinement increases grain-boundary density and creates stronger barriers to dislocation motion.
Nanoscale precipitates act as strong obstacles to dislocation motion.
Combined grain-boundary and dispersion strengthening will increase hardness and compressive yield strength.
The ductile matrix will remain sufficiently interconnected after processing to maintain plasticity.
Relative to the cast alloy, the ball-milled and spark-plasma-sintered alloy will show a statistically significant increase in hardness and compressive yield strength.
The processed alloy will maintain ductility or experience only a moderate reduction in ductility up to 600 °C.
The controlled comparison uses the same equimolar Co-Cr-Fe-Ni-Ti composition for a conventionally cast control and a ball-milled, vacuum-SPS-processed test material.

The hypothesis is limited to equimolar CoCrFeNiTi tested in compression from room temperature through 600 °C and excludes substantially different compositions, extreme strain rates, and higher temperatures.
